questions.q: Why does this lab's scenario rule out centralized governance for the Employee Service Center rollout?
options: Finance's heavy approval chain and Marketing's near-frictionless flow can't both be served correctly by the same single review queue
Finance's requirements are technically impossible to implement under any governance model
Centralized governance is never a valid choice for any ServiceNow rollout
Marketing has no legitimate need for a review process of any kind
questions.explain: One centralized setting would either over-control Marketing's low-risk requests or under-control Finance's regulated-spend requests — there's no single correct answer for both.

questions.q: Why does the lab pilot the Employee Service Center with Marketing rather than Finance?
options: Finance's requirements are impossible to build at all
Marketing's use case is the simplest, so a clean pilot win there builds confidence before the harder, higher-stakes Finance rollout
Pilot department choice should always default to whichever department asks first
Marketing is funding a larger share of the project than Finance
questions.explain: Lesson 26's sequencing rule picks the pilot by contained use case, not by size or funding share — Marketing's simpler flow is the better first proof point.

questions.q: In the finished design, what is built once as the SHARED piece across all eight departments?
options: The base intake form, the underlying data model, and the notification framework
Finance's specific multi-step approval chain, reused unchanged by every department
A separate Employee Service Center instance per department
Each department's own approval routing logic
questions.explain: The base intake experience is built once and shared; approval routing is where departments genuinely differ, so that part is built department-specific.

questions.q: In the executive pitch to the CFO and department heads, how is the federated-governance decision framed?
options: Using technical terms like "federated governance" and "department-specific extensions" directly
As a purely technical decision that doesn't require executive approval
As a request for unlimited budget with no specific cost or risk explained
One build serving every department instead of eight separate systems, with Marketing getting speed and Finance keeping its required approval chain, at a known shared-team cost
questions.explain: The underlying decision, cost, and risk stay the same — only the vocabulary changes so the budget-holding audience can actually evaluate and defend it.

questions.q: What guardrails from Lesson 25 does this lab say must be actively enforced across all eight departments for federation to work here?
options: One naming convention, mandatory code review, and a shared component library
A separate sys_domain for each of the eight departments
A requirement that every department use identical approval routing
No guardrails are needed once a pilot department has succeeded
questions.explain: Those three guardrails are what keeps federated autonomy from reproducing duplicate builds and inconsistent conventions across eight departments.
